pages.title: CSS Positioning - static and relative
pages.content:
- The **position** property in CSS decides how an element is placed on the page. By default, every element follows the normal flow of the document - one after another, top to bottom. But with positioning, you can shift elements around in more flexible ways.
---
1. **position: static; (The Default)**  
   - This is the **default value** for all elements.  
   - The element stays in the **normal document flow** (stacked like blocks or inline as usual).  
   - You **cannot move it** with `top`, `left`, `right`, or `bottom` properties.  
   - Think of it as: “Just stay where the page naturally puts you.”  
   - Example: A paragraph with `position: static;` will appear right after the previous element, like normal text.

2. **position: relative; (The Shifter)**  
   - The element still **stays in the document flow** (it takes up its normal space).  
   - But you can now **shift it** using `top`, `left`, `right`, or `bottom`.  
   - Importantly: The space it originally occupied is **still reserved**.  
   - Think of it as: “Stay in your place, but move a little without disturbing others.”  
   - Example: A box with `position: relative; top: 20px; left: 10px;` will look like it has “slid” down and to the right - but the space it left behind is still there.
---

pages.title: Absolute & Fixed Positioning
pages.content:
- CSS positioning lets you place elements exactly where you want them.  
- Now we’ll explore **absolute** and **fixed**, which give you much more control than static or relative.
---
1. **position: absolute; (The Breakaway)**  
   - The element is **removed from the normal document flow** (it no longer reserves space).  
   - It is positioned **relative to its nearest positioned ancestor** (the closest parent with `position: relative`, `absolute`, or `fixed`).  
   - If no such ancestor exists, it positions itself relative to the entire **page (document body)**.  
   - You can use `top`, `left`, `right`, and `bottom` to place it exactly where you want.  
   - Example:  A box with `position: absolute; top: 20px; left: 30px;` will float **20px from the top** and **30px from the left** of its positioned container (or the page if no parent is positioned).

2. **position: fixed; (The Sticker)**  
   - The element is also **removed from the normal flow**.  
   - It is positioned **relative to the viewport** (the visible screen area), not to a parent.  
   - This means it **stays in the same place even when you scroll**.  
   - Great for making sticky headers, navigation bars, or “back to top” buttons.  
   - Example: A button with `position: fixed; bottom: 10px; right: 10px;` will always stay in the **bottom-right corner** of the screen, no matter how much you scroll.

pages.title: Position - Sticky
pages.content:
- Sticky positioning is a mix between relative and fixed.  
- An element with `position: sticky` behaves like relative until you scroll past a certain point, then it sticks to a position like fixed.  
- This is useful for headers, table headings, or navigation bars that you want to remain visible only after scrolling to a certain point.
---
**Key Points:**

- It requires a `top`, `bottom`, `left`, or `right` value to define where it sticks.  
- It stays within its parent container, unlike fixed which is relative to the viewport.  
- Until the element reaches the sticky point, it behaves like a normal relative element.

**Use Cases:**
- A table header that stays visible while scrolling through rows.  
- A sidebar that becomes fixed when you scroll down a long page.
---
**Syntax:**
```dfwef
.sticky-element {
position: sticky;
top: 10px; /* sticks 10px from the top when scrolling */
}
```

pages.title: Z-Index & Stacking Order
pages.content:
- When you have **multiple elements overlapping** on a page, which one appears on top? That’s where **z-index** comes into play.  
- Think of your elements like **cards stacked on a table**.  
  - The card on top is fully visible.  
  - The cards underneath are partially or completely hidden.  
- In CSS, **z-index** controls which “card” is on top.
---
**Key Points:**

**1.Higher Z-Index = On Top**  
  - Elements with a higher `z-index` value appear **above** elements with a lower value.  
  - Example: `z-index: 10` will appear above `z-index: 5`.

**2.Position Matters**  
  - `z-index` only works on elements that have `position` set to `relative`, `absolute`, `fixed`, or `sticky`.  
  - Static elements ignore `z-index`.

**3.Stacking Context**  
  - Each positioned element can create a **stacking context**, which is like a mini-layered world inside itself.  
  - Elements in one stacking context don’t automatically stack with elements outside of it.
---
**Example**\
Imagine three boxes: **Red**, **Green**, **Blue**.  
- If all boxes are overlapping, the one with the **highest z-index** will appear on top.  
- If two boxes have the same z-index, the one that appears **later in HTML** will be on top.

pages.title: Flex Container & Flex Items
pages.content:
- Flexbox (short for **Flexible Box Layout**) is one of the most powerful tools in CSS for arranging elements.  
- Instead of struggling with floats, margins, or positioning, Flexbox lets you easily align and distribute space between elements.

---
**Flex Container**\
To start using Flexbox, you first declare a parent element as a **flex container**.
```sdfwef
.container {
display: flex;
}
```
- This makes `.container` a **flex container**.  
- All the direct child elements inside it automatically become **flex items**.
---
**Flex Items**\
The elements inside the flex container are called **flex items**.  
- They sit next to each other in a row by default.  
- They can stretch, shrink, or align depending on the container’s settings.
---
**Controlling Layout with Flexbox**
- **justify-content** → controls how items are spaced horizontally (main axis).
  - Example: justify-content: space-around; spreads items evenly with space around them.
- **align-items** → controls how items are aligned vertically (cross axis).
  - Example: align-items: center; centers items vertically inside the container.

Together, these two properties give you precise control over positioning without needing extra hacks.

pages.title: Flex Sizing
pages.content:
- Flexbox not only helps arrange items but also controls how much space each item takes inside a container. This is where flex sizing comes in.
---
1. **flex-grow**  
Determines how much an item can grow relative to other items when there’s extra space in the container.  
Example: `flex-grow: 2;` → this item will grow twice as much as an item with `flex-grow: 1`.

2. **flex-shrink**  
Determines how much an item can shrink relative to other items when space is limited.  
Example: `flex-shrink: 0;` → this item won’t shrink even if the container gets smaller.

3. **flex-basis**  
Sets the initial size of a flex item before growing or shrinking.  
Can be in pixels, percentages, or auto.  
Example: `flex-basis: 200px;` → the item starts at 200px, then grows or shrinks based on available space.
---
**Shorthand: flex**\
You can combine all three properties in one line:
```dfwef
.item {
flex: 1 0 200px; /* flex-grow | flex-shrink | flex-basis */
}
```

- `1` → grow factor  
- `0` → shrink factor  
- `200px` → initial size

pages.title: Grid Container & Items
pages.content:
- CSS Grid is a layout system that helps you place items in **rows and columns** at the same time. It’s like giving your page a neat table-like structure, but with way more flexibility.

**1. The Grid Container**
- To start, you need a **parent element** that holds your grid. You turn it into a grid with:
```wdfw
.container {
display: grid;
}
```
Once you do this, all the direct children inside become **grid items**.

----
**2. Defining Rows and Columns**
- The most important part of Grid is deciding how many **rows** and **columns** you want:
```wdweqcd
.container {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 200px 200px 200px; /* 3 columns */
  grid-template-rows: 100px 100px;          /* 2 rows */
  /* You can also use repeat() to shorten this, e.g., grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 200px); */
}

```

This gives you a grid with **3 columns** and **2 rows**.  
- Each column is **200px** wide.  
- Each row is **100px** tall.  
- Items will automatically fill these cells one after another.
---
**3. Grid Items**
- Any child element inside the grid container becomes a **grid item**.  
- By default, they fill the cells **from left to right, top to bottom**, like this:
```wdcw
1 | 2 | 3
4 | 5 | 6
```

You want to create a 10px space between the product cards horizontally and a 20px space between them vertically.\
Which of the following CSS declarations would achieve this?

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Use css grid to write clear, maintainable CSS for the target user interface.

codeCard.code: .features { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); gap: 24px; }
